In this class the teacher counts out loud, and the whole room moves on the count.
One breath, one move.
Inhale, lift. Exhale, lower and hold. Inhale, chest up. Exhale, hips up. Inhale, jump through and sit.
This is an intermediate class... but everyone can start from zero.
Want to try a class with us in Bangkok? Comment TRIAL and we'll message you.

Want to try a class with us in Bangkok? Comment TRIAL and we'll message you.

caption:
Our teacher ranks 10 hard asanas, from 1 (easiest) to 10 (hardest). They come from the intermediate series, the second set of asanas in Ashtanga yoga.
Seven headstands get only a 3. Kapotasana, a deep backbend, gets a 9, because it can get harder as your body changes.
Number 10 is Karandavasana. It needs strong arms, strong belly muscles, and flexible hips and legs.
None of these is too far away. Your body and skills grow little by little, with good guidance and your own dedication (you keep showing up).
From our Saturday led class with @boonchutanti. Led means the teacher counts and the whole room moves together.
Want to try a class with us in Bangkok? Comment TRIAL and we'll message you.
#aybkk #ashtanga #ashtangabangkok #yogabangkok #bangkokyoga #intermediateseries #karandavasana #boonchutanti
truth_notes: Video: 2:04 talking-head tier list. The teacher, in a red AYBKK tank top, sits outside by a pool, with class clips in a box. 0-4.9 s is a wide shot of the room. Burned in for the whole video: the title 'Rank how difficult the asanas in intermediate series.' plus the 10-to-1 list on the left, with word-by-word subtitles in the clip box. What he says (Whisper, asana names corrected by me): 1 is easiest, 10 is hardest. Pincha 4 ('everyone's favorite'). Bakasana A easy, B very tough, 5. Pasasana 1 ('should be the easiest because you already passed Marichyasana D'). Kapotasana 9 ('gets difficult as your body changes'). Supta urdhva pada vajrasana 7 ('people roll up and don't hold the feet'). The seven headstands 3 ('Mukta hasta C is the most difficult if you do it properly with locked elbows, but the rest are easy'). Mayurasana 8 (hard to hold straight and level). Titibhasana 2 (hamstrings are already flexible by then). Dwi pada sirsasana 6 (many can't point the feet out). Karandavasana 10 ('requires the core and arm strength and also hip and legs flexibility'), shown with a crown on the list. Nakrasana is spoken at the end as 6.5 and is not on the list. Original caption (26 Aug 2026): 'The most difficult 10 asanas in intermediate series. These asanas is not too far to reach with gradual development of your body and skills with proper guidance and your dedication. Saturday led intermediate @boonchutanti'. Draft hook: '10 hardest' is supported by that caption. 'Still in reach' is supported by the caption ('not too far to reach'), not by anything spoken in the video. No claim is unsupported. Some clips (for example the Kapotasana close-ups) look like other rooms or days. The 'Saturday led intermediate' credit comes from the original caption.

caption:
It's Saturday, and this is our led class. Led means the teacher counts the breaths and the room follows the count.
These asanas come from Advanced A, the third set of asanas in Ashtanga yoga.
Then the hard part comes, like a handstand. No second thoughts. You just do it, and you hold it.
The teacher walks the room and helps. Here he helps a student find bandha, a gentle lift low in the belly.
Alone, it is easy to skip the hard part. With the room around you, you keep going.

caption:
After two babies, our teacher @missjamsai found her lower back weak and her belly muscles stretched out.

With no belly strength to hold her up, deep backbends could hurt her lower back. So she had to go carefully.

Her fix starts with bandha: holding the belly in from the inside, without squeezing the abs too hard.

Then she lifts her chest and keeps her shoulders low instead of arching her lower back, and she uses her shoulders to pull herself back up.

Stretch and stay strong at the same time. And be patient with your body.

Clips from our led class (the teacher counts the breaths for the whole room), plus old clips from when she was pregnant.

Want to try a class with us in Bangkok? Comment TRIAL and we'll message you.

truth_notes: Video is 1:56, posted 14 Dec 2024. @missjamsai talks to camera in English (brick wall, Ashtanga tee) about backbending after pregnancy. What she says: after pregnancy her lower back was very weak; carrying the big belly stretched everything; there was no core or abdominal strength to pull her back up; it took 2-3 months to feel her abs again; she had to be careful not to hurt her lower back; her psoas was very tight; she holds bandha all the time, but bandha is not over-contracting the abs, and bandha alone is not enough for deep backbends. Her examples are Ganda Bherundasana and tic-toc (control the ribcage). Her main problem is tight hips. You can't just hang the legs without support or you may hurt your back. Connect the upper body and use the shoulders to pull back up. Stretch and contract at the same time ('dynamic'). Lift the chest, keep the trapezius down, don't arch the lower back. It ends with her laughing and the burned text '[THAI] IT'S DIFFICULT TO EXPLAIN.' then '[THAI] CAN I SPECK THAI?'. caption:
Flexibility isn't about forcing.

Your muscles have tiny sensors inside. Stretch too fast, and the muscle tightens on its own to protect itself.

So rushing into an asana starts the very thing that stops you.

Slow breath, long holds, the same asanas every day. Your body learns it is safe and stops fighting.

A good teacher takes you to your edge, not past it.

Filmed at our workshop in Huizhou, China, with @boonchutanti.

Want to try a class with us in Bangkok? Comment TRIAL and we'll message you.

caption:
'I don't want to wake up early.' 'It's too hard.' 'Everyone there is so good.' Most people who say this haven't even tried yet.

@boonchutanti sees 5 levels when people try something new: I can do it. If others can, I can too. Let's try and see. I tried, it didn't work. No way, I know myself.

Most people stop before level 3, the one where you simply give it a try.

At level 4 or 5 right now? That's OK. What matters is being open to moving up.

Start where you are, with small steps, one at a time. Even if you tried before.
